item.title: The picture is not the proof. The paperwork is.
item.description: Photographs no longer carry their own credibility. Provenance does — the RAW original, the capture record and a licence signed by the maker.

item.title: The three tests every frame has to pass
item.description: Provenance, not reproducible by a machine, and a named buyer. A frame has to clear all three before it is catalogued.

item.title: What actually goes on an accession label
item.description: The fields on a catalogue record, why each one is there, and the three buyers ask about long after the campaign has ended.

item.title: Two days aboard before the first frame
item.description: Why the fisher plate could not be photographed on day one, and what changes once nobody is performing for the camera.

item.title: Pricing a licence when the buyer says “just for social”
item.description: Media, term and territory are three separate questions. “Just for social” answers none of them, and it is rarely meant unkindly.

item.title: Who actually buys photography in Norway
item.description: Thirty industries in four tiers, from agencies buying weekly to recruiters discovering employer branding, and the ten worth contacting first.

item.title: How long blue hour actually lasts at 59° north
item.description: A computed field table of twilight length by month at 59° north, and the received wisdom it contradicts.

item.title: Seven pictures worth avoiding at launch
item.description: Aurora over wilderness, fjord at sunset, the perfectly composed cabin. Technically fine, commercially finished.

item.title: Content credentials, switched on from the first frame
item.description: Why provenance metadata has to be enabled in camera, and why signing a file afterwards convinces nobody who matters.

item.title: The filing habit that makes an archive findable in nine years
item.description: RAW archived within 24 hours, release signed within 7 days, catalogue decision within 14. Dull on purpose.
